memory_update.content: For the New Hotspots theme, prioritize candidates with direct exposure to AI data-center execution bottlenecks: electrical infrastructure, mechanical/electrical contracting, optical interconnect, high-density cooling, and firm-power supply-chain constraints.
Demote broad demand-side or diversified beneficiaries when public-market purity is low, even if evidence quality is high; use hyperscalers mainly as capex and procurement signal sources.

For contractors and HVAC names, next checks should focus on data-center revenue mix, backlog segmentation, project-level evidence, margin contribution, labor constraints, and whether exposure is AI-specific rather than general commercial construction.

For optical names, next checks should focus on AI data-center design wins, customer concentration, component scarcity, CPO or high-speed transceiver exposure, capacity utilization, and margin trajectory.

For nuclear names, next checks should separate near-term nuclear supply-chain revenue from long-duration advanced-reactor narratives, with emphasis on licensing, fuel, binding customers, deployment timing, and policy dependence.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need project-level disclosure or backlog segmentation showing data-center mechanical/electrical work, margin contribution, customer concentration, and whether growth is from AI-scale facilities rather than general commercial construction.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Mechanical and electrical contracting capacity maps directly to the practical execution layer of data-center buildout, including power distribution, cooling systems, and facility commissioning. This is close to the validated theme that electrical infrastructure and project execution, not only chips, are constraining AI infrastructure deployment.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need clearer data-center revenue mix, backlog by end market, project duration, labor availability, and evidence that data-center margins are structurally better than broader construction/services work.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: EMCOR is a direct second-order beneficiary if electrical and mechanical project execution capacity becomes scarce for large-load data centers. Its relevance increases where substations, backup power, electrical rooms, cooling loops, and facility services become gating items for energized capacity.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need customer-specific validation, AI data-center revenue exposure, margin recovery evidence, capacity utilization, and proof that Coherent controls scarce components rather than participating in a competitive transceiver/component cycle.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Coherent maps to optical materials, lasers, and optical communications components, which are plausible chokepoints as AI clusters require faster intra-data-center and inter-data-center links. The optical-interconnect node has high demand durability if AI networking bandwidth intensity continues rising.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need direct linkage between data-center firm-power procurement and BWXT-addressable work, including reactor component orders, fuel-service demand, customer commitments, timing, and whether near-term revenue is actually driven by commercial power rather than government nuclear programs.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: BWXT has scarce nuclear component and fuel-services exposure. If firm power becomes a durable AI data-center constraint and nuclear deployment or life-extension activity accelerates, nuclear-grade manufacturing, components, and services could become hard-to-replicate supply-chain nodes.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence of AI data-center design wins, customer concentration, product-level margin improvement, capacity constraints, and whether Lumentum's exposure is to the fastest-growing AI optical layers rather than slower telecom or legacy optical demand.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Lumentum is a plausible AI networking and photonic-components beneficiary. Optical components are structurally relevant as AI clusters increase bandwidth intensity, and the company could be positioned near scarce laser or photonic component supply if customer qualification evidence improves.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need segment-level proof of data-center infrastructure exposure, customer programs, power-product backlog, margin profile, and whether Flex captures bottleneck economics or mainly volume-based assembly economics.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Flex may benefit from manufacturing, power-products, and data-center infrastructure demand if OEMs and hyperscalers need scalable outsourced production. It ranks below purer chokepoint suppliers because contract manufacturing usually has lower control over final bottleneck economics.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need project-level verification tying EPC backlog to data-center power, nuclear, gas, transmission, or industrial infrastructure specifically driven by AI load growth.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Fluor has EPC exposure to advanced nuclear, industrial infrastructure, and power projects. It is relevant if time-to-power and firm-generation buildout become central to data-center siting, but the AI linkage is indirect and project timing can be long.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need contracted HALEU volumes, funding certainty, licensing progress, production ramp evidence, customer commitments from reactor developers, and proof that AI firm-power demand accelerates rather than merely narratively supports the business.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Centrus has high-beta exposure to uranium enrichment and HALEU, a potential gating item for advanced nuclear deployment. It scores highly on bottleneck and supplier scarcity but is penalized for policy dependence, timing uncertainty, and indirect linkage to AI data-center power demand.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need data-center-specific order growth, liquid-cooling or high-density cooling product exposure, backlog, margins, and proof that Trane is participating in scarce AI facility thermal systems rather than general HVAC replacement demand.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Trane has credible thermal-management exposure, and rising AI rack density could increase demand for specialized cooling. However, public-market purity is diluted by broader HVAC exposure, and the company needs data-center-specific evidence to move higher.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need data-center revenue segmentation, high-density cooling exposure, controls attach rate, backlog, and evidence that data-center demand materially changes growth or margins.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Johnson Controls has possible exposure through HVAC, controls, fire/security, and facility infrastructure. It is relevant to data-center buildout but ranks lower because the exposure is diluted and may not capture the most constrained parts of the AI infrastructure stack.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need separation of data-center cooling revenue from general commercial HVAC, evidence of high-density or liquid-cooling relevance, margin impact, and customer/project validation.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Carrier has broad HVAC and thermal-management exposure that could benefit from data-center cooling demand. It ranks below more focused contractors and optical/nuclear chokepoint names because direct AI data-center purity and evidence quality are weaker.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need evidence that data-center power procurement causes incremental nuclear fuel demand beyond existing reactor fleet dynamics, restart schedules, utility contracting, and broader uranium-cycle factors.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Cameco maps to uranium mining, conversion, and nuclear fuel services. It is relevant if AI data-center firm-power demand increases the strategic value of nuclear generation, but the linkage is upstream, commodity-sensitive, and less directly tied to data-center deployment bottlenecks.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need procurement-level data linking Amazon capex and power agreements to specific supply-chain beneficiaries; Amazon itself is too broad to isolate the New Hotspots chokepoint economics.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Amazon is a high-quality demand-side signal for AI compute, data-center capex, power procurement, and co-located generation structures. It is useful as an evidence source but less attractive as a Serenity chokepoint candidate because it is a diversified hyperscaler rather than a scarce bottleneck supplier.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need licensing milestones, NRC progress, fuel supply, binding customer contracts, site readiness, cost evidence, financing capacity, and credible deployment timelines.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Oklo is a pure public-market mapping to the advanced nuclear and firm-power-for-data-centers narrative. It remains a research node because licensing, deployment timing, fuel availability, and revenue validation are still early-stage relative to the current data-center power bottleneck.

ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need licensing progress, reactor design validation, fuel supply, binding customers, credible deployment timeline, financing evidence, and proof of commercial relevance to data-center firm-power demand.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Nano Nuclear Energy is a speculative public-market proxy for microreactors and advanced nuclear enthusiasm. It has narrative purity but very weak current evidence relative to Serenity standards because commercial deployment, licensing, fuel, customers, and economics remain unvalidated.

summary: Within this candidate chunk, the highest Serenity research priority goes to names closest to validated AI data-center execution bottlenecks: mechanical/electrical contractors, nuclear supply-chain components, optical interconnect suppliers, and power/cooling infrastructure enablers. Lower priority is assigned to broad HVAC names with diluted exposure, demand-side hyperscalers, upstream commodity nuclear fuel, and early-stage advanced nuclear developers where evidence, timing, licensing, and public-market purity are weaker.
